searchText: > "subroutines are part of every Virtual Machine I have seen" In some form, under some name, yes. OO machines like JVM have message dispatch to do the job. > we didn't want to invest the time into something that will just be swept away based on ever changing feelings This is the precedent I don't want to keep reinforcing. Groups refrain from doing work because they can't count on ACD following through on decisions, even long-standing decisions. Which deprives us of the experience needed to make good decisions. > Groups refrain from doing work because they can't count on ACD following through on decisions Groups _should_ do work to provide strong evidence to ACD that their feature proposal solves critical problems. If groups refrain from doing work, it could be a signal that the feature is is not very useful. On modern hardware, subroutines are implemented by pushing the return address to the operand stack, then jumping. Interestingly, ARM (optional) and RISC-V (required) have jump opcodes which designate a link register to which it saves the return address (next opcode) to. This allows skipping the stack. But I am guessing that most calling conventions will use the stack anyway, since the link register will be clobbered by subsequent jumps. The RISC-V manual says "Return-address prediction stacks are a common feature of high-performance instruction-fetch units." So an optional second stack is useful in hardware instruction fetch. Have we established one way or another whether we have a "consumer/user" for subroutines as they are implemented or on an eventual upgrade that brings them closer to the original EIP-615 functionality? I haven't followed the full conversation, but the comments I've seen from the solidity team suggest they won't use them in the current form. Fe-lang likely follows suite since they leverage the same IR as solidity. There is one potential consumer who has not implemented anything in it yet. Sometimes I think that something is a good idea until I start implementing it. Then I realize that it should be another way. who/what is this potential consumer? Vyper is the potential consumer. kk Have any of the compiler maintainers mentioned anything about whether EIP-615 subroutines would be more desirable? Leaving us where we are now - considering backing out of a decision at the 11th hour, further diminishing that trust. Maybe the feature just isn't that important. It doesn't seem to solve any critical problems. I'll refer back to my previous comment, it we think that a compiler should have at least provisional implementation of a feature like this before it goes live, and that should block activation, then I can see that logic. It we don't want to create that kind of block, and there's strong enough evidence in the EIP to justify activation, then we activate. If we want to remove it from this fork, it needs to be postponed To postpone is probably to kill - I've little time or energy left for this years-long effort. If we're just going to go back and forth ad nauseum, I have better things to do with my time. Sometimes I think that something is a problem, then I start to think about it, and that problem disappears as new problems arise. After a while, I eventually arrive at critical problems. Exactly, <@!659892951006183425>. We've spent years designing, discussing, implementing, and testing this. It's the first step in a long-planned program of EVM improvement. Reopening the technical discussion at this stage, on this channel, is not likely to lead to anything new - at least not by Friday. So I need to get to work on what I'm paid to do. Carry on. > It's the first step in a long-planned program of EVM improvement. Please share a link to your program. It will give us important context. See EIP-615 EIP-615 has a different meaning for "subroutines". The same can be said about `JUMP` and `JUMPI` though - in the case of off by one error you'll get a revert if you don't jump to a `JUMPDEST`. I suspect that the 2 adaptations that were made to subroutines actually removed most of their usefulness. 1) having `JUMPSUB` to take the destination from the stack means it no better for static analysis than other jumps, 2) no protection from inter-jumps eliminates the "first in/first out" property of subroutines in our usual understanding. Also no protection from inter-jumps erodes potential safety benefits. so it sounds like we have a goldilocks situation: EIP-615 was too much at one time, and EIP-2315 is too little? so in order for EIP-2315 to be useful, it basically needs to look like EIP-615, which was too much at once, so it needs to be small like EIP-2315, but that's not useful so we need more... (ad infinitum) If you want to arrive at EIP-615, then perhaps EIP-2315 should have immediates for BEGINSUB and JUMPSUB. Phasing in EIP-615 by churning through opcodes with EIP-2315 seems reckless. Or maybe you will keep EIP-2315 opcodes, but then we don't add much value. I am not sure what the "long-planned program of EVM improvement" is. > long-planned program of EVM improvement It meant to add subroutines in the EIP-615 sense (with EIP-2315 intended as a stepping stone to reach that eventual goal) The feedback that ultimately "cancelled" EIP-615 was that it was too complicated to be done all at once, and that's how we ended up with EIP-2315 so, if people feel there is no path to subroutines (in the EIP-615 sense) from EIP-2315, I would say it's not performing the job it was meant to perform I don't believe that is the case, but that's above my paygrade at this point apparently <@!682078300234973185> > If you want to arrive at EIP-615, then perhaps EIP-2315 should have immediates for BEGINSUB and JUMPSUB. We have been through this already. Years ago. Immediate data is not backwards compatible. That means EVM versioning. That is non-trivial, and not on the table at this time. And again. This EIP is old. It's been under discussion for years. It's ready to deploy. Hashing over questions that have already been discussed is not helpful. Imposing new requirements this late in the game is not helpful. Please, please, please. Show some respect. I've gathered my thoughts from last night here, hope it will help someone: https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/263#issuecomment-790423785 yes If neither you nor anyone else has implemented any prototype using this, how are you (and others) so certain this is the way to go? As <@456226577798135808> and <@!427011130318389248> pointed out, it might actually be safer to *not* use them. One interesting thing that is happening just now, is that several people are voicing their purely technical concerns about the EIP. The EIP at first was claiming gas benefits, which were now removed. A Solidity team member reported a counter gas analysis on the same example, without any magic, refuting it. This triggered the much used response "Solidity should have objected earlier". Well, why didn't *anyone* do that earlier? Why were the EIP claims not verified before acceptance? I'm not referring to specific people here, rather the opposite, just showing that anyone could have done that, yet it wasn't done (myself included). Maybe is time to define how "freezing" is managed wait three months more and someone doing research will found a cool way to redefine subroutines I don't want to interfere in the decision process about what to do right now in any way, but I'd be *very* happy to help in considering how to improve the situation and potentially end up with subroutines Solidity *could* use without having to pay more for it than is gained, if at all possible and if there will be time and opportunity for it. Is there a recommended way for wallets to automatically build access lists for EIP-2930? It seems like an `eth_getAccessList` rpc endpoint would be useful I think Geth has one, I don't know what it is though. Perhaps their docs have been updated with it? not anything I could find... https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/pull/22289 I'm still working on it amazing, thanks For me this is important statement, it seems that standalone EIP-2315 is not useful even for Vyper and probably is not going to be used and it is meant as stepping stone, if I got that right? Then I am now looking at EIP-2315 as part of EIP-615 and not standalone EIP, and in that sense would it not make sense to include it as whole when time comes and work is done on complete change? I'd very much be interested in any concrete plans to build up something like EIP-615 on top of EIP-2315 to be able to judge how that affects my analysis, so if anyone can point me to any concrete documentation about that, I'd be very thankful! Such plans would need a champion. I will not be that champion. I have offered the Ethereum community the very best proposals I know how to make, at considerable expense of my own and other people's time, effort, and expertise. These proposals have been under review for years now. EIP-2315 has - over the course of the last year - been accepted, implemented, tested, and scheduled for this very upgrade. I have nothing more to offer. **AllCoreDevs in ~23h (Friday March 5th, 14:00 UTC)** **Agenda**: https://github.com/ethereum/pm/#acd-107-march-5-2021 **Stream**: https://youtu.be/xWfR-WxjmYg Even with some increased cost, if the proposal makes it easier for us to implement internal methods safer, in some sense of the word "safer", and puts us on the upgrade path to full "subroutines" (in the EIP-615 sense) we would likely adopt. A 5% gas cost hike for increased safety is worth it, even if the safety improvement is marginal, and especially it there is some bytecode reduction as well because bytecode size is a bigger problem for us than cost. I do agree that the intention to traverse to "full subroutines" (in the EIP-615 sense) must be taken into consideration, and if ACD has no cohesive strategy to do so after many years of attempts by this author (and considerable pain), then that makes this proposal less useful. Suggestions to "just add a stack rotation opcode" might be an alternative to EIP-2315 that provides some marginal benefit, but marginal benefit should not take precedence over having a holistic approach to the upgrade to "full subroutine functionality" (in the EIP-615 sense) The problem here is a lack of focus Having learnt from this, if we continue on the EIP-615 path after Berlin, I will provide very strong opposition until an actual problem that needs solving has been identified. "We need subroutines" is not a problem to be solved - it is a proposed solution to an unstated problem. Once we know what we want to achieve and have agreed that it is a worthwhile goal, we can all work together on a purely technical discussion on how to achieve that goal best. Also "we don't want dynamic jumps" is lacking the definition of a dynamic jump, a reason why we don't want dynamic jumps and a justification why there are no other means to work with the jumps we already have. Fwict there is no agreed upon plan / strategy towards full 615. 2315 is either worth it standalone or not worth it, imo. I'm listed as a co-author on 2315, but mainly because it was approved and I wanted to ensure it was as good as it could be, but I'm not a 'champion' for it. My main motivation for supporting it now is because it's a decision already made. I won't attend ACD on Friday, but I am fine with whatever is decided. excerpts.author: gcolvin
excerpts.content:
> "subroutines are part of every Virtual Machine I have seen"
In some form, under some name, yes.  OO machines like JVM have message dispatch to do the job.

excerpts.author: gcolvin
excerpts.content:
> we didn't want to invest the time into something that will just be swept away based on ever changing feelings
This is the precedent I don't want to keep reinforcing.  Groups refrain from doing work because they can't count on ACD following through on decisions, even long-standing decisions.  Which deprives us of the experience needed to make good decisions.

excerpts.author: pauld.9606
excerpts.content:
> Groups refrain from doing work because they can't count on ACD following through on decisions

Groups _should_ do work to provide strong evidence to ACD that their feature proposal solves critical problems. If groups refrain from doing work, it could be a signal that the feature is is not very useful.

excerpts.author: pauld.9606
excerpts.content: On modern hardware, subroutines are implemented by pushing the return address to the operand stack, then jumping.

excerpts.author: pauld.9606

This allows skipping the stack. But I am guessing that most calling conventions will use the stack anyway, since the link register will be clobbered by subsequent jumps.

excerpts.author: pauld.9606
excerpts.content: The RISC-V manual says "Return-address prediction stacks are a common feature of high-performance instruction-fetch units." So an optional second stack is useful in hardware instruction fetch.

For now we only found a way to speed up execution by about 7% for contracts where we prove there are no invalid jumps possible. excerpts.content:
Yesterday evening one point was brought up: it is safer to detect stack corruption bugs with returnsub.

If I understand correctly, if the stack is corrupted before return (has more or less items than expected), then using RETURNSUB, the callee (where we return to) will have some weird values, but will progress onwards and then likely fail somewhere else. Contrary to this, with JUMP, if the return address (the top stack item) is wrong, it is very likely the jump will lead to a non-jumpdest and fail outright, aiding locating of the issue.

Can you please explain the safety benefits you see of EIP-2315’s current version of returnsub?
